posters.title: Shop bot, answer or hand off
posters.story: As a small shop owner running a website and phone bot, I want the bot to answer what its configured facts cover and hand everything else to staff, so customers never hear an invented price, stock level or booking.

explained.why: Same accuracy as the LLM (88 against 86 of 100) at about a fifth of the cost per kept answer.
explained.next: Open the 100-message run, or try your own decision.
explained.earlier: 40 messages: tied 38 to 38, Not proven yet (LLM was Haiku 4.5).

run.question: Can the bot answer this customer message using only the fact sheet, or must it hand off to staff?
run.reason: use Jev: Jev is within 10 points of the LLM (lower bound -0.04) and costs 0.197 of it per accepted answer (upper bound 0.218)
run.headline: At least as accurate as the LLM (88/100 vs 86/100) at 1/4th of the cost

posters.title: CV against a job ad
posters.story: As a hiring manager I want each CV checked against each line of my job ad, so I read the strong ones first and stop paying an LLM to reread every CV in full.

explained.why: Only 5 CVs are labelled. The rules need at least 30 before they compare Jev with the LLM.
explained.cases: Jev 5 of 5, the LLM 5 of 5, the simple rule 2 of 5. Jev spent $0.00008 against the LLM's $0.0109.
explained.next: Label 25 more CVs against the same ad line.
explained.rephrase: "Rank these CVs" is a written judgement, so Jev probably not. Ask one yes/no per ad line instead: "Does the CV show the person has built or run a product that pools AI subscriptions or tokens?" Code adds up the lines to rank (pattern P2).

figures.quote: on at least 30 paired Jev and rule cases

posters.title: Requirement evidence check
posters.story: As a builder before a demo I want each requirement in my spec checked against the evidence I hold for it, so I know which ones are met, partly met or not met without rereading everything.

explained.why: No cases have been run yet, so there is nothing to compare.
explained.next: 20 or more requirement and evidence pairs, each labelled met, partly met or not met by hand.
explained.rephrase: Where a test or check script exists, its exit code decides "met", and Jev adds nothing. Where the evidence is prose, ask: "Does this evidence excerpt support this requirement? met / partly met / not met" (pattern P1).

posters.title: Tech stack choice
posters.story: As a user I want Jev to decide on my tech stack for my project.

explained.why: No cases have been run. "Decide my tech stack" is open design work that needs reasoning and a written answer, which Jev does not do.
explained.next: 20 or more project descriptions, each labelled by hand with the properties it needs.
explained.rephrase: Ask yes/no per property instead: "Does this project need realtime updates?" (and the same for relational joins, row-level access, self-hosting, offline-first, file storage). A written mapping table, not Jev, turns the answers into the stack (pattern P2).

posters.title: Website slop roast
posters.story: As a website builder I want to use Jev!Jev to roast and score my website as AI slop so that I can fix it and win awards for awesome web apps.

explained.why: No cases have been run. "Is this AI slop?" is an open question with no fixed answer set.
explained.next: a labelled set of real sites, each check marked by hand, before any score is published.
explained.rephrase: Ask one check at a time with a fixed answer, for example "Is the headline generic marketing filler? 0 / 1 / 2" or "Does the hero use a purple-to-blue gradient? yes / no". Code weights the answers into the score (pattern P3). Jev reads text only, so visual checks need the page text or CSS.
